title: CPSC 541 - Chapter 5: Establishing the Business Requirement

questions.question: Which level of requirements is the highest level of abstraction?
options: Functional requirements specify detailed software behavior and sit below the user and business levels.
User requirements capture what people must accomplish, but they are not the top level of abstraction.
Business requirements are the highest level of abstraction and set direction for all lower requirement levels.
Interface requirements describe connections to other systems rather than the project's top-level business need.
Quality attributes state how well the product must operate instead of defining the highest business goals.
Test requirements list later verification checks and do not sit at the top of the requirements chain.
questions.explanation: Business requirements are the top-level requirements. User and functional requirements are subordinate to them.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: Business requirements represent the top of the requirements chain. They define the vision of the solution and the scope of the project that will implement the solution.
reference.lecture: In summary, in Chapter 5, we talked about top-level requirements, which is known to be a business requirement. Again, business requirement consists of two major components. One is product vision and project scope.

questions.question: User requirements and functional requirements should support the project's business objectives.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that lower-level requirements should not be included if they do not address the business objectives.

reference.section: Business requirements drive the lower levels
reference.excerpt: The user requirements and functional requirements must align with the context and objectives that the business requirements establish. Requirements that don't help the project achieve its business objectives shouldn't be implemented.
reference.lecture: Welcome to chapter 5. In this chapter, chapter 5, we'll talk about then how to establish the top level of requirements. Remember, there are three levels of requirements. The top one was business requirements, then user requirements, and function requirements.

questions.question: Why is it important for stakeholders to share the same understanding of business objectives?
options: Shared objectives require every stakeholder to adopt the same programming language before work can start.
Shared objectives keep project participants aligned instead of pulling the work in conflicting directions.
Shared objectives freeze the requirements so that no stakeholder may request a change later in the project.
Shared objectives let developers implement the product without further conversation with customers or users.
Shared objectives make testing unnecessary because they already guarantee that the delivered product is correct.
Shared objectives require every proposed feature to receive equal priority regardless of business value.
questions.explanation: A shared understanding of business objectives helps keep project participants aligned instead of pulling the project in conflicting directions.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: The vision provides the context for making decisions throughout the product's life, and it aligns all stakeholders in a common direction. Project participants can unwittingly work at cross-purposes if they have different objectives and priorities.
reference.lecture: So, if you look at slide 8, it shows product vision, and slide 9 shows the scope of the project. Final slide 10 shows the business context, such as stakeholders, project priorities, and also deployment consideration. So, again, slides 8 through 10 show the template of vision and scope documents.

questions.question: According to the lecture, business requirements consist mainly of which two components?
options: Business requirements consist mainly of a detailed design model together with a complete implementation plan.
Business requirements consist mainly of a testing strategy together with a deployment checklist for operations.
Business requirements consist mainly of the product vision together with the scope of the current project.
Business requirements consist mainly of a roster of named users together with the developers assigned to code.
Business requirements consist mainly of a feature backlog together with the source code that will implement it.
Business requirements consist mainly of a budget spreadsheet together with a staffing plan for the team.
questions.explanation: The professor emphasizes that business requirements consist primarily of product vision and project scope.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: Two core elements of the business requirements are the vision and the scope. The business requirements consist of mainly two parts: one is the vision, and the other one is scope.
reference.lecture: In this chapter we're going to talk about business requirements. The business requirements consist of mainly two parts. One is the vision, and the other one is scope.

questions.question: What does the product vision describe?
options: The product vision describes how source files and modules will be organized inside the implemented software.
The product vision describes the ultimate long-term goal of the product and the destination being pursued.
The product vision describes the exact functions that must ship in the next release and nothing beyond that.
The product vision describes the test cases and schedules the team will use to verify the next increment.
The product vision describes who will be hired and how the team will be staffed for this particular release.
The product vision describes the defects currently open in the tracker rather than the product's destination.
questions.explanation: The product vision describes the long-term direction or ultimate goal for the product.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: The product vision succinctly describes the ultimate product that will achieve the business objectives. The vision describes what the product is about and what it ultimately could become.
reference.lecture: Now, the product vision describes, if you will, the long-term goals of the products, whereas the scope describes mainly short-term objectives, such as what part of the vision is addressed at this time. questions.question: The product vision generally changes slowly over time.
questions.explanation: Because it represents the long-term goal, the product vision is relatively stable compared with the project scope.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: The vision should change relatively slowly as a product's strategic positioning or a company's business objectives evolve over time. Scope is more dynamic than vision.
reference.lecture: Now, the product vision describes, if you will, the long-term goals of the products, whereas the scope describes mainly short-term objectives, such as what part of the vision is addressed at this time. questions.question: What does project scope primarily describe?
options: Project scope describes the company's long-term future strategy rather than what this project will deliver now.
Project scope describes the short-term objective and which part of the vision this project or release will address.
Project scope describes the finished source-code architecture developers must produce before any release ships.
Project scope describes every feature the product might ever include across all future releases and markets.
Project scope describes only the testing strategy the team will follow and not which capabilities are in scope.
Project scope describes the business's legal corporate structure instead of the boundary of the current trip.
questions.explanation: Scope identifies the portion of the broader product vision that a particular project or release will address.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: The project scope identifies what portion of the ultimate product vision the current project or development iteration will address. The statement of scope draws the boundary between what's in and what's out for this project.
reference.lecture: In summary, in Chapter 5, we talked about top-level requirements, which is known to be a business requirement. Again, business requirement consists of two major components. One is product vision and project scope.

questions.question: A project's scope typically covers:
options: Project scope normally covers every release the product will ever have, from the first increment through retirement.
Project scope normally covers one release of the product, or one iteration toward the longer product vision.
Project scope normally covers only the user-interface screens and ignores other capabilities planned for release.
Project scope normally covers only the business rules and leaves features, data, and interfaces outside the boundary.
Project scope normally covers only nonfunctional qualities such as speed and ignores functional work for the release.
Project scope normally covers only future product ideas that have not yet been accepted for any planned increment.
questions.explanation: The slides state that project scope normally applies to one product release.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: The scope pertains to a specific project or iteration that will implement the next increment of the product's functionality. Project scope normally applies to one product release.
reference.lecture: In summary, in Chapter 5, we talked about top-level requirements, which is known to be a business requirement. Again, business requirement consists of two major components. One is product vision and project scope.

questions.question: Which constraints can cause project scope to be adjusted? Select all that apply.
options: Project cost limits can force the team to reduce what the current release is able to include.
The release schedule can require shrinking the portion of the vision this trip will cover.
Available resources can cause the planned contents of a release to be scaled back later.
Agreed quality targets can require trimming scope so remaining work still meets the bar.
The lead developer's favorite color can dictate which capabilities belong in this release.
Available team capacity can limit how much of the product vision this project can deliver.
questions.explanation: Scope must adapt to practical constraints such as cost, schedule, resources, quality, and available capacity.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: Stakeholders adjust the contents of each release within its schedule, budget, resource, and quality constraints. Scope must account for cost, schedule, resources, and quality.
reference.lecture: In summary, in Chapter 5, we talked about top-level requirements, which is known to be a business requirement. Again, business requirement consists of two major components. One is product vision and project scope.

questions.question: Which statement best explains the difference between vision and scope?
options: Vision is the short-term release plan, while scope is the unchanging long-term destination of the product.
Vision defines the long-term product direction, while scope defines what part of that vision this project addresses.
Vision describes how the source code is structured, while scope describes only the tests that will be run.
Vision and scope are two names for the same idea and can be used interchangeably in every project document.
Scope becomes meaningful only after the product has already been deployed and users are working in production.
Vision is a concern only for developers writing code and does not guide sponsors or other business stakeholders.
questions.explanation: Vision describes where the product is ultimately going; scope defines what the current project will actually tackle.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: The product vision ensures that we all know where we are hoping to go eventually. The project scope ensures that we are all talking about the same thing for the immediate project or iteration.

questions.explanation: Different stakeholders naturally have different priorities, so conflicts should be expected and managed.

Users are the stakeholders typically associated with wanting predictability and profit from the project.
Developers are the stakeholders typically associated with wanting simplicity above all other technical interests.
Managers are the stakeholders typically associated with wanting predictability and profit from the project.
Sponsors are the stakeholders typically associated with wanting convenience only and no funding role.
Users are the stakeholders typically associated with controlling project funding rather than using features.
questions.explanation: The slides associate managers with predictability and profit.

reference.excerpt: Different stakeholders want different things: customer wants simplicity, user wants convenience and features, developer might want interesting technology, and manager wants predictability and profit.

questions.question: Which pair correctly reflects common stakeholder interests from the slides?
options: Customers often want simplicity, while users often want convenience together with additional product features.
Customers often want maximum technical complexity, while users often want fewer features than they have now.
Developers often want predictability and profit, while managers often want experimental technology first.
Sponsors often want to avoid decisions, while users often want exclusive control over project funding choices.
Managers often want simplicity above all, while customers often want access to the product source code.
Developers often want fewer features delivered, while users often want the project to operate with lower staffing.
questions.explanation: The chapter uses this contrast to show why business requirements can conflict.

questions.question: Who is responsible for resolving conflicts involving business stakeholders?
options: Any individual developer may settle business-level conflicts without involving sponsors or other decision makers.
The project sponsor is responsible for resolving conflicts among business stakeholders when they cannot agree.
Only the tester may decide how competing business objectives should be traded off for the current release.
Only the end user may resolve conflicts among business stakeholders, including funding and priority disputes.
The database administrator decides which stakeholder goals survive when business requirements are in conflict.
The newest team member is expected to settle sponsor-level conflicts because that person is not yet biased.
questions.explanation: The sponsor is responsible for resolving business-level conflicts when stakeholders cannot all be satisfied.

reference.excerpt: The project's decision makers must resolve these conflicts before the analyst can detail the requirements. The project sponsor resolves major business-level conflicts.

questions.question: Why can stakeholder conflict not always be solved by satisfying everyone?
options: Everyone cannot be satisfied because every documented requirement is automatically wrong and must be discarded.
Everyone cannot be satisfied because stakeholders can have competing goals and constraints that cannot all be met.
Everyone cannot be satisfied because developers should ignore users and implement whatever technology looks fun.
Everyone cannot be satisfied because project scope never matters when people disagree about desired features.
Everyone cannot be satisfied because business objectives are optional and need not guide which requests are kept.
Everyone cannot be satisfied because customers do not influence requirements and therefore cannot create tension.
questions.explanation: Different stakeholders can have incompatible priorities, so tradeoffs are often required.

reference.excerpt: The tension among stakeholders with different goals and constraints can lead to clashing business requirements. Not everyone gets everything.
reference.lecture: So, if you look at slide 8, it shows product vision, and slide 9 shows the scope of the project. questions.question: Business requirements can influence which aspects of use cases? Select all that apply.
options: Business requirements influence how many use cases are included in the system planned for this effort.
Business requirements influence how extensively each accepted use case should be implemented in the release.
Business requirements influence the relative priority of each use case when the team sequences the work.
Business requirements influence which developer's IDE must be installed before any use case can be specified.
Business requirements influence which stated business goals the selected use cases are expected to support.
Business requirements influence whether a given use case belongs in the current release or should be deferred.
questions.explanation: Business requirements guide which use cases are included, how much of them is implemented, and their relative priority.

reference.section: Business requirements drive the lower levels
reference.excerpt: Business requirements guide which use cases belong in the system, which use cases are most important, and how extensively they should be implemented. They directly influence which user requirements to implement and in what sequence.

questions.question: A use case that does not support any business objective should automatically be included because users requested it.

questions.question: How many vision and scope documents should normally exist for the project, even if multiple systems will be developed?
options: A separate vision and scope document should be written for each developer who will work on the project.
A separate vision and scope document should be written for each system even when they share one vision.
A single vision and scope document should normally exist for the project, even if several systems are built.
A separate vision and scope document should be written for each stakeholder so that no views are combined.
A separate vision and scope document should be written for each release candidate the team considers later.
No vision and scope document is needed when the project is large enough to have several cooperating systems.

questions.question: Who owns the vision and scope document?
options: The project sponsor owns the vision and scope document as the executive or funding authority for the work.
Any developer on the team owns the vision and scope document and may change business direction at will.

The user-interface designer owns the vision and scope document because screens define the product vision.
The help desk owns the vision and scope document because support staff hear every complaint after release.

questions.question: Who may provide input into the vision and scope document? Select all that apply.

questions.question: Why are limitations and exclusions useful in a scope document?

They make all future changes impossible, locking the product so that no later release may add any work.
They replace project priorities such as constraints, drivers, and degrees of freedom for the whole effort.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a context diagram?
options: It shows the system and how it interacts with external entities through information or material flows.

It calculates the project's cost, schedule, and staffing without describing any system boundary at all.
It creates the acceptance tests that customers will run after the product has already been constructed.
It shows only internal database tables and omits external entities that exchange data with the system.

reference.excerpt: The context diagram visually illustrates the boundary. It identifies external entities outside the system that interface to it, as well as data, control, and material flows between those terminators and the system.
reference.lecture: Final slides 11, 12, 13, and 14 describe the techniques, how to represent the scope of the project. Initially, slides 11 and 12 show so-called a context diagram. A context diagram basically shows how a system, software system, interacts with the so-called external entities of that system in terms of data that are being exchanged, or known to you as a context diagram or flow diagram, if you know what a flow diagram is.

questions.question: In a context diagram, the main system is shown together with:
options: The main system is shown together with external interfaces and the information or material flows exchanged.
The main system is shown together with only the source-code files developers will create for internals.
The main system is shown together with only the user-interface screens and no other external entities.
The main system is shown together with a list of developer tasks rather than neighboring entities and flows.
The main system is shown together with executed test results instead of external entities and exchanged data.
The main system is shown together with project budgets rather than information flowing across the boundary.
questions.explanation: The diagram shows the system in relation to external entities and the information exchanged with them.

reference.excerpt: The entire system is depicted as a single circle. The external entities can represent user classes, organizations, other systems, or hardware devices, and the arrows represent flows between the system and those entities.
reference.lecture: Final slides 11, 12, 13, and 14 describe the techniques, how to represent the scope of the project. Initially, slides 11 and 12 show so-called a context diagram. A context diagram basically shows how a system, software system, interacts with the so-called external entities of that system in terms of data that are being exchanged, or known to you as a context diagram or flow diagram, if you know what a flow diagram is.

questions.question: In the Chemical Tracking System example, the chemist sending a request for a chemical to the system is an example of:
options: It is an information flow between an external entity and the system, as a context diagram would show.
It is a business risk about marketplace timing rather than a flow drawn across the system boundary.
It is a project priority expressed as a constraint, driver, or degree of freedom for the current release.
It is a success metric used to judge whether the project is on track to meet its business objectives.
It is a feature-tree branch that decomposes Order Chemicals into Search and Chemical Request work.
It is a developer constraint about staffing or tools rather than an exchange with an outside actor.
questions.explanation: The professor uses this example to explain how context diagrams show external entities exchanging data with the system.

reference.excerpt: The arrows on the diagram represent the flow of data, such as a request for a chemical, between the system and its external entities. A chemist uses the chemical tracking system by sending a request for a chemical.
reference.lecture: If you look at, for example, slide number 12, it shows the interaction between the chemist and the system. That is, a chemist uses the chemical tracking system by sending a request for a chemical. So, there is interaction between chemist and also tracking system by sending a request for a chemical.

questions.question: What does an ecosystem map primarily show?
options: It shows how the system's related components or subsystems interact with one another across the solution.
It shows only the system's user-interface screens and ignores other systems that interconnect with it.
It shows only the business goals and does not depict related systems or the nature of their interactions.
It shows only a single use-case path and does not map the wider network of participating systems.
It shows only external customers as people and omits the other systems that may need modification.
It shows only deployment servers and hosting sites rather than systems that interconnect and exchange data.
questions.explanation: An ecosystem map provides a broader graphical view of related systems or components and their interactions.

reference.excerpt: An ecosystem map shows all of the systems related to the system of interest that interact with one another and the nature of those interactions. It provides a broader graphical view of related systems or components.
reference.lecture: The Ecomap basically is a graphical representation of how the individual components of your system interact with each other. So, for example, slide 13 shows the components initially of the chemical tracking system and it shows how they interact with each other. So, all the subsystems, if you will, of your system and how they interact with each other.

questions.question: A context diagram and an ecosystem map are exactly the same representation.
questions.explanation: A context diagram emphasizes the system boundary and exchanges with external entities, while an ecosystem map shows the wider network of interacting systems or components.

reference.excerpt: Ecosystem maps differ from context diagrams in that they show other systems that have a relationship with the system you're working on, including those without direct interfaces. A context diagram emphasizes the system boundary and exchanges with external entities.
reference.lecture: Then, system provides a vendor catalog if the chemical needs to be ordered. So, the context diagram shows the overview of the system in terms of external entity and how these external entities exchange data with the system. Slide 13 shows a technique called Ecomap, or ecosystem map.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a feature tree?
options: A feature tree decomposes major product features into smaller supporting features arranged in a hierarchy.
A feature tree displays project salaries and compensation bands instead of the product's planned capabilities.
A feature tree stores test results from verification runs rather than showing how features break into parts.
A feature tree replaces all requirements documents so that no vision, scope, or SRS text is needed anymore.
A feature tree shows only external systems and their interfaces, which is the job of context or ecosystem views.
A feature tree determines programming-language syntax rules instead of refining large features into sub-features.
questions.explanation: A feature tree breaks larger capabilities into smaller related sub-features.

reference.excerpt: A feature tree is a visual depiction of the product's features organized in logical groups, hierarchically subdividing each feature into further levels of detail.
reference.lecture: Finally, slide 14 shows a feature tree where you can identify the major features along with sub-features that are necessary to accomplish these major features. So, for example, slide 14, you will see a feature called order chemical, which is on the top right-hand side. Hopefully, you see that.

questions.question: The lecture describes a feature tree as a form of step-by-step refinement from larger abstractions to smaller ones.
questions.explanation: The professor explicitly explains feature decomposition as refining a larger abstraction into smaller supporting abstractions.

reference.excerpt: You have initially a big abstraction and then you use step-by-step refinement to find small abstractions that accomplish that bigger abstraction. A feature tree breaks larger capabilities into smaller related sub-features.
reference.lecture: So, again, in order to accomplish search feature, you need to have three sub-features that accomplish that particular feature. If you will, you're basically doing the so-called step-or-step refinement. That is, you have initially a big abstraction and then you're using step-or-step refinement to find small abstractions that accomplish that particular bigger abstraction.

questions.question: In the Chemical Tracking System feature tree, 'Order Chemicals' is an example of:
options: Order Chemicals is a major feature that can be broken into sub-features such as Search and Chemical Request.
Order Chemicals is a business risk about chemical costs rather than a capability shown on the feature tree.
Order Chemicals is a stakeholder profile describing chemists instead of a feature branch on the product tree.
Order Chemicals is a success metric for order time rather than a major feature decomposed into supporting parts.
Order Chemicals is a deployment consideration about lab locations rather than a feature with Search beneath it.
Order Chemicals is a context-diagram interface to vendors rather than a feature-tree node for ordering work.
questions.explanation: The lecture uses 'Order Chemicals' as an example of a major feature that is decomposed into smaller features.

reference.excerpt: The gray boxes represent the L1 features, such as Order Chemicals. Search and Chemical Request are subfeatures of Order Chemicals.
reference.lecture: Finally, slide 14 shows a feature tree where you can identify the major features along with sub-features that are necessary to accomplish these major features. So, for example, slide 14, you will see a feature called order chemical, which is on the top right-hand side. Hopefully, you see that.

questions.question: Why is breaking a large feature into smaller sub-features useful?
options: Breaking a large feature down helps explain what smaller capabilities are needed to accomplish that larger feature.
Breaking a large feature down guarantees the project has no defects because every sub-feature is automatically correct.
Breaking a large feature down eliminates the need to define scope because the tree already lists every future release.
Breaking a large feature down prevents requirements from changing, since a decomposed feature can never be adjusted.
Breaking a large feature down replaces business objectives so that feature names become the only success measure.
Breaking a large feature down allows developers to ignore stakeholders because the tree substitutes for their input.
questions.explanation: Feature decomposition helps analysts understand the smaller capabilities required to realize a larger business capability.

reference.excerpt: A feature tree hierarchically subdivides each feature into further levels of detail. Feature decomposition helps analysts understand the smaller capabilities required to realize a larger business capability.
reference.lecture: Finally, slide 14 shows a feature tree where you can identify the major features along with sub-features that are necessary to accomplish these major features. So, for example, slide 14, you will see a feature called order chemical, which is on the top right-hand side. Hopefully, you see that.

questions.question: What is scope creep?
options: Scope creep is uncontrolled growth of project scope as more functionality is added without disciplined control.
Scope creep is a planned reduction in requirements that shrinks the release through an approved tradeoff.
Scope creep is a testing technique for finding defects by exercising the product at the system boundary.
Scope creep is a problem that occurs only when a context diagram uses the wrong shape for the system.
Scope creep is a user class or market segment rather than a failure to keep the project boundary in focus.
Scope creep is a deployment strategy for rolling the solution out to locations, not a growth of the scope.
questions.explanation: Scope creep occurs when more and more functionality is added without disciplined scope control.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Keeping the scope in focus
reference.excerpt: Many projects suffer from scope creep—rampant growth as more and more functionality gets stuffed into the product. The goal of scope control is to prevent uncontrolled scope creep while still accommodating evolving needs.
reference.lecture: Now, the product vision describes, if you will, the long-term goals of the products, whereas the scope describes mainly short-term objectives, such as what part of the vision is addressed at this time. Also, the business requirement ultimately influences the user requirements, the next level, which are expressed in terms of, we'll look at those later, in terms of use cases. So, lecture-wise, if you look at slides 8 through 10, they show the templates of such vision and scope documents, which you can see also in our project case for COS, or it's the cafe ordering system.

questions.question: Keeping scope under control means refusing all new requirements.
questions.explanation: The chapter says teams should prevent uncontrolled scope creep while still accommodating evolving needs.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Keeping the scope in focus
reference.excerpt: A scope definition is a structure, not a straitjacket. Scope change isn't a bad thing if it helps you steer the project toward satisfying evolving customer needs; uncontrolled scope change is the problem.
reference.lecture: Final slides 11, 12, 13, and 14 describe the techniques, how to represent the scope of the project. Initially, slides 11 and 12 show so-called a context diagram. A context diagram basically shows how a system, software system, interacts with the so-called external entities of that system in terms of data that are being exchanged, or known to you as a context diagram or flow diagram, if you know what a flow diagram is.

questions.question: What are the three possible decisions for a newly proposed requirement? Select all that apply.
options: Decide that the request is in scope, so keep it and consider it among the committed work for this effort.
Decide that the request is out of scope, so discard it or defer it instead of forcing it into this release.
Decide that the request is out of scope but valuable enough to justify changing the scope on purpose.
Decide that the request should be implemented automatically as soon as any stakeholder writes it down.
Decide that the request should always be delayed until the next project, even when it is clearly in scope.
Decide that the request should be judged while ignoring the business objectives that define valuable work.
questions.explanation: The slides give exactly these three possible decisions for evaluating a proposed requirement against the project's scope.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Keeping the scope in focus
reference.excerpt: Remember, whenever someone requests a new requirement, the analyst needs to ask whether it is in scope. The three outcomes are keep an in-scope request, reject or defer an out-of-scope request, or intentionally change the scope when the idea is valuable enough.
reference.lecture: Final slides 11, 12, 13, and 14 describe the techniques, how to represent the scope of the project. Initially, slides 11 and 12 show so-called a context diagram. A context diagram basically shows how a system, software system, interacts with the so-called external entities of that system in terms of data that are being exchanged, or known to you as a context diagram or flow diagram, if you know what a flow diagram is.

questions.question: A proposed feature does not fit the current scope but strongly supports the business objectives. What is one valid response?
options: Change the project scope through an appropriate decision process, accepting the tradeoffs that follow.
Add the feature secretly so that sponsors and other stakeholders never see the written boundary move.
Ignore all cost and schedule impact and insert the work without adjusting any other project dimension.
Automatically reject it solely because it is currently outside the written scope statement for this release.
Ask a developer to build it without approval from the people who own the project's scope decision.
Remove the vision statement so that the new feature no longer needs any business justification at all.
questions.explanation: If an out-of-scope requirement is valuable enough, the project may deliberately change its scope rather than allowing uncontrolled scope creep.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Keeping the scope in focus
reference.excerpt: The third possibility is that the proposed new requirement is out of scope, but it's such a good idea that the scope should be broadened to accommodate it, with corresponding changes in budget, schedule, and/or staff.
reference.lecture: Now, the product vision describes, if you will, the long-term goals of the products, whereas the scope describes mainly short-term objectives, such as what part of the vision is addressed at this time. Also, the business requirement ultimately influences the user requirements, the next level, which are expressed in terms of, we'll look at those later, in terms of use cases. So, lecture-wise, if you look at slides 8 through 10, they show the templates of such vision and scope documents, which you can see also in our project case for COS, or it's the cafe ordering system.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes Chapter 5?
options: Business requirements define the long-term vision and current project scope, align lower-level requirements with business objectives, and provide techniques for documenting and controlling scope.

Business requirements are mainly about source-code architecture and module layout rather than vision, scope, alignment of lower-level work, or techniques for documenting and controlling the project boundary.
The chapter focuses only on user-interface layout and visual design rather than establishing business requirements, aligning lower-level needs, modeling scope, or keeping that scope under control.
The chapter explains how to eliminate all requirement conflicts so every stakeholder preference can be satisfied without tradeoffs, a sponsor decision, or any remaining tension among business goals.
The chapter focuses entirely on writing and executing tests rather than vision, scope, the vision and scope document, scope models, or techniques for keeping the project boundary in focus.
Business requirements apply only after implementation is finished and cannot guide scope, alignment of lower-level requirements, documentation, or control decisions during requirements development.
questions.explanation: Chapter 5 is about establishing the top-level business requirements through product vision, project scope, supporting documentation, scope models, and scope control.

reference.book: Chapter 5 — Product vision and project scope
reference.excerpt: Business requirements explain why the organization is building the product. Two major parts are product vision and project scope, and the chapter also covers the vision and scope document, scope models, and scope control.
reference.lecture: In summary, in Chapter 5, we talked about top-level requirements, which is known to be a business requirement. Again, business requirement consists of two major components. One is product vision and project scope.
